newsitem.title: BELGIUM: AFRICAN GSM CALLS GO THROUGH BELGIUM.
newsitem.headline: AFRICAN GSM CALLS GO THROUGH BELGIUM.

text.p: Ringing your mate in Madagascar on your mobile from Morocco? You might be surprised to find your telephone call has been routed through a U.S.-owned satellite centre in Belgium.
The centre, called Afrilink, is the brainchild of U.S. private telecommunications services provider Telecel, which discovered a niche in connections between Africa and Europe.
The operation has been a roaring success. Created in 1995, it had 1996 turnover of 36 million Belgian francs.
In a recent interview with Reuters, manager Jean-Louis Parmentier forecast a rise in turnover to 40 to 45 million in 1997 when Afrilink expects to post its first, slight, profit.
In addition to GSM services, both between African countries and between the African and European continents, the network allows for picture and data transmision.

High-speed data and multiple voice lines are used through Intelsat 325 and 359 space links. Afrilink's network also allows for calls to North America and the rest of the world, all through its network control centre in Belgium.

"The geographic situation of Belgium, in the middle of Europe, is very interesting for us because it keeps transmission costs down. We have also chosen Belgium because of the opportunity to get public aid", Parmentier told Reuters.

On Afrilink's $2 million investment in 1996 in the satellite centre in Charleroi, south of Brussels, it received subsidies from the European Union and Wallonia, the southern region where it is located, amounting to 30 percent of the total.

It is counting fresh EU assistance for another $2 million package to develop more satellite connections between Europe, the U.S. and several countries in Africa and install more high-tech equipment in 1998.

Afrilink has cooperation agreements with European public phone companies, such as Belgacom of Belgium, BT of Britain and Dutch Koninklijke PTT Nederland, to carry GSM calls and other signals from Europe to Africa.
"We have actually a leading position in western Europe (in satellite telecomms services to Africa)", Parmentier said.
It is more cost effective for the public carriers to use Afrilink's existing network than to set up their own.
In the private sector it has added video tele-conferencing to its list of services. Clients include Coca-Cola Co.
Parmentier expects Afrilink to go from strength to strength. It currently employs five people and it sees staffing more than doubling to 12 at the end of the next year.
Capitalised at 30 million francs, Afrilink prefers to remain privately-owned, although Parmentier does not rule out a stock market listing in the next few years.
